OF VICTIMS OF THE PARKLAND SHOOTING AS

STATEMENT OF INTEREST1
Amici are survivors and family members of victims
of the mass shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas
High School in Parkland, Florida, on February 14,

1 No party or counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or
in part. No party, counsel for a party, or person other than amici
curiae or their counsel made any monetary contribution intended
to fund the preparation or submission of this brief.

2


2018. They have experienced firsthand the devastating impact that an assault weapon can have, allowing
one man to murder or injure more than 30 students
and teachers in under 10 minutes. Amici are committed to working to prevent anyone from experiencing
the same trauma they have and have a vital interest
in ensuring that the Constitution is interpreted correctly to allow the enactment of gun-violence-prevention measures that will protect themselves, their
classmates, their families, and all Americans.
Aalayah Eastmond was a junior at Stoneman Douglas and in a Holocaust history class in Classroom
1214—the third classroom that the gunman targeted—on February 14. She survived by hiding under
the body of Nicholas Dworet, who was shot and killed
along with others in her class. She is now an outspoken activist against gun violence and is a founding
member of Team ENOUGH at Brady United. She
joins this brief in her individual capacity.
Jaclyn Corin was a junior at Stoneman Douglas. On
the day of the shooting, she spent hours trapped and
hiding in her classroom, fearing that the gunman
might target her class next. She is also an activist
against gun violence and is the current Executive Director of March for Our Lives. She joins this brief in
her individual capacity.
Robert Schentrup is the brother of Carmen
Schentrup, who was killed in Classroom 1213 in her
AP Psychology class. He is also an activist against gun
violence and is a founding member of Team ENOUGH
at Brady United.  He joins this brief in his individual
capacity.

3


Ivy Schamis was a history teacher at Stoneman
Douglas and was teaching her History of the Holocaust class in Classroom 1214 when the gunman fired
into the room, killing two of her students. She is a
member of Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence. She
joins this brief in her individual capacity.
Mitch and Annika Dworet are the parents of Nicholas Dworet, a senior and gifted swimmer who was
killed in Classroom 1214, and of Alex Dworet, who
was wounded in the shooting.
Anthony Borges was a freshman at Stoneman Douglas who was shot five times while using his body to
hold a classroom door closed against the gunman. He
was the most gravely wounded survivor and received
the Congressional Medal of Honor Society’s Young
Hero Award in 2019.
Stephanie Horowitz was a freshman at Stoneman
Douglas who hid in a classroom closet for more than
two hours and lost four friends in the shooting. She is
now a law student at Tulane.
Fred Guttenberg is the father of Jaime Guttenberg,
a 14-year-old student who was killed in the shooting.
He has dedicated his life to ending gun violence.
All amici file this brief in their personal capacity and
not on behalf of any organization.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
This Court recognized in District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 595 (2008) that the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms is “not unlimited.”
Nor has the right ever been viewed as “a right to keep

4


and carry any weapon whatsoever in any manner
whatsoever and for whatever purpose.” Id. at 626.
New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen later established a framework to determine whether conduct
is “rooted in the Second Amendment’s text, as informed by history” and so is constitutionally protected. 597 U.S. 1, 19 (2022). That framework requires
determining, first, whether “the Second Amendment’s
plain text covers an individual’s conduct,” and, second, whether “the regulation is consistent with this
Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” Id.
at 17. The Court should find for Respondents at either
step.
Assault weapons fall outside the Second Amendment’s presumptive protection. The Amendment protects weapons “ ‘in common use’ today for self-defense.” Id. at 32. As Heller emphasized, self-defense is
“the central component of the right” to keep and bear
arms, 554 U.S. at 599, and “weapons that are most
useful in military service—M-16 rifles and the like—
may be banned,” id. at 627.
AR-15-style weapons share the M-16’s core design
and are almost never used for lawful self-defense. See
Cook Cnty. Br. 2-3, 36-38, 53; Conn. Br. 24, 32-33.
Even to the extent they are “Arms” because they are
“customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes,”
Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. 185, 195 (2026), it is their
offensive, military character that makes them so, rather than any common use for lawful self-defense.
In all events, as Respondents explain, the restrictions on assault weapons in these cases are independently sustained by the Nation’s historical tradition of regulating unusually dangerous weapons. In

5


making that assessment, the Court should look at
“how and why the regulations burden a law-abiding
citizen’s right to armed self-defense.” Bruen, 597 U.S.
at 29. This is particularly important in cases—such as
these—that implicate “unprecedented societal concerns” or “dramatic technological changes” different
from those in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Id. at 27.
As the Parkland survivors and families know all too
well, AR-15s and other similar weapons can be used
to carry out mass shootings. There is no evidence that,
at the time the Second Amendment was drafted, any
firearms could be used to carry out mass shootings.
“From 1791 through the mid-nineteenth century, the
ubiquitous firearm was a single-shot, muzzle-loaded
firearm,” and the few repeating arms of the era were
“technologically flawed curios with limited practical
utility.” Barnett v. Raoul, 180 F.4th 1035, 1055-1056
(7th Cir. 2026). The unprecedented change in technology that allowed for the creation of modern assault
weapons has created equally unprecedented societal
concerns. As a result, the Court should conclude that
there is no constitutionally protected right to possess
AR-15-style assault rifles.
Ultimately, however, we leave the law to the parties
and other amici.
On February 14, 2018, a gunman armed with an AR-
15-style rifle entered Marjory Stoneman Douglas
High School in Parkland, Florida. He opened fire in
the school’s 1200 building, and, in less than ten
minutes, he killed 17 students and staff members and
wounded 17 others. The attack became the deadliest
mass shooting at a high school in United States

6


history. We write in this case to tell the stories of those
who died, those who were wounded, and those were
left behind to carry their legacies.
What started out as an ordinary Valentine’s Day
quickly turned into death and destruction spread
across classrooms and hallways. In a matter of
minutes, lives were lost, survivors sustained devastating physical and psychological injuries, and families
and an entire community were left to confront enduring grief and trauma.
Petitioners would have this Court hold that a firearm’s perceived popularity determines whether the
Second Amendment protects the right to own it. That
“popularity” based rule is not required by the Constitution and would lead to shootings like Parkland over
and over again. Assault weapons are weapons of war,
and governments should be free to enact bans to keep
these dangerous weapons out of civilian hands.
ARGUMENT
The stories that follow recount February 14 through
the experiences of teachers and students who were inside the school and families who lost loved ones. Together, their accounts illustrate both the catastrophic
destructive capacity of assault weapons and the lasting human consequences of their use in a mass shooting.
A. Aalayah Eastmond
From a young age, Aalayah Eastmond was intimately aware of the horror and lasting impact gun violence can cause. When she was a child, her uncle was
shot and killed in Brooklyn, New York. Although
Aalayah was too young to understand what was going

7


on at the time, she saw how the tragedy affected her
mother. Because of that experience, Aalayah was
aware that gun violence was an unfortunate reality
that she personally could face at any point.
But Aalayah had no idea that she would become a
survivor of a school shooting when she arrived at campus on February 14, 2018. The day began like any
other. There was a fire drill that morning, during
which Aalayah remembers hearing conversations
about the need for a school shooting drill as well.
Aalayah’s last period that day was Ms. Schamis’s
history class in room 1214. Aalayah was seated near
the door, which she worried would be distracting. As
she worked on an independent-study lesson, she
heard several loud noises. She did not know what the
noises were at first, but she knew immediately that
something was wrong.
Those loud noises were the first shots fired outside
of Aalayah’s classroom. When the second set of shots
went off, Aalayah and her classmates tried to hide in
the corners of the room. Unfortunately, with more
than 30 students, there was not enough space for everyone to hide.
Aalayah made it to a corner, diagonal across from
the classroom door. Another student, Aalayah’s friend
Helena Ramsay, began passing around books from a
bookshelf for Aalayah and her classmates to use to
shield their heads from bullets.
Even as she prepared to shield herself, Aalayah
thought that the noises might be part of a really
messed up senior prank. When she saw red liquid
pooling on the floor, she thought it was red paint from

8


a paintball gun. Then she saw Helena slump over on
the ground and Aalayah began to understand the reality of what was happening.
Terrified that she would die, Aalayah watched as
another classmate, Nicholas Dworet, began to tilt towards the ground. She mimicked the movements of
Nick’s body as she fell to the ground underneath him.
Aalayah told herself that she would hold her breath if
someone came by and kept waiting to see the shooter’s
boots appear on the ground next to her.
The shooter moved away from classroom 1214.
Aalayah’s classmates started to check pulses of the
others in the room to see who was injured and who
was dead. Aalayah’s friend pulled her behind the podium in the front of the room for safety.
Aalayah saw that one of her friends was clearly injured. She texted her friend’s mother to let her know.
Aalayah then called her own parents to say her last
goodbyes. She told her parents she was sorry for anything she had done that might have upset them.
Finally, police officers entered the room. The officers
told the students to run out of the building as fast as
they could and instructed them not to look up or down.
As Aalayah ran out of the building, she passed the
bodies of three more of her fellow students.
When Aalayah got outside, complete chaos had
erupted around her. Barefoot, she walked over to a
Walmart a few minutes away from the school. Police
officers near the Walmart grabbed Aalayah and began
picking body matter out of her hair and placing it in a
bag as evidence. The officers then brought Aalayah
back to the very place she had just fled and took her

9


into an evidence truck parked outside Building 1200.
The officers had Aalayah take off her clothes and
change into a hazmat suit as they asked her to recount
everything that had just happened. Finally, hours
later, Aalayah’s mother picked her up from the Marriott ballroom where she was waiting with other students and the families of those still missing.
Immediately following the shooting, Aalayah was
scared by everything. She even remembers feeling terrified when her own beloved dog poked its head into
the room. Aalayah spent weeks sleeping with her
mother in the same bed because she did not feel safe
even in her own home.
In the wake of the shooting, Aalayah’s mother encouraged her to speak out about her experience. Her
mother told Aalayah that by sharing her story, she
might help others in similar situations. Years later,
Aalayah continues to do so. She now lives in Washington, DC and dreams of becoming an attorney. Aalayah
believes that while her experience surviving a school
shooting is unfortunately not unique to her, it should
be. She cautions that unless a change is made, this
country will continue to watch young people die by
firearms. Now is the time for change, by imposing restrictions on assault weapons like the one that was
used to kill and maim Aalayah’s fellow classmates.
B. Ivy Schamis
Ivy Schamis grew up in North Miami Beach, Florida, and moved to Parkland in 1995. She and her husband were drawn to the close-knit, welcoming community as a place to raise their two children, who later
attended Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School.
Ms. Schamis began teaching at the school in 2001 and

10


took great pride in its strong academics, extracurricular activities, and school spirit.
February 14, 2018, began as a wonderful day. Students were in a festive mood that Valentine’s Day, carrying flowers and boxes of chocolates. That afternoon,
Ms. Schamis was teaching her fourth-period History
of the Holocaust class in Room 1214, on the ground
floor of the school’s 1200 building. Because the Winter
Olympics were underway, she had planned a lesson
on the 1936 Berlin Olympics.
With about 20 minutes of class remaining, Ms.
Schamis and her students heard loud, unmistakable
gunshots in the hallway. The students looked to her
and then scattered to different corners of the crowded
classroom, crouching beneath desks and behind furniture. The school had not conducted an active-shooter
drill, and some students initially wondered whether
the sounds were part of an exercise. The room offered
no meaningful place to hide: a long glass panel ran
down the classroom door, making the students easy
targets, lined up like ducks.
Earlier that day, during an administrative meeting,
teachers had been reminded to keep their classroom
doors locked. Although Ms. Schamis had not routinely
locked her door before then, she did so that afternoon.
Within seconds of the first shots, gunfire shattered the
door’s glass panel and entered the classroom. Ceiling
tiles fell, and the room descended into chaos as students tried to move books and furniture for protection.
Ms. Schamis watched the damaged door and feared
that the shooter would enter.
Ms. Schamis recalls hearing screams, gunfire, and
prayers, as well as shots in the classroom across the

11


hall, where a colleague and friend taught. Cell service
was poor, making it difficult to reach 911, but Ms.
Schamis was able to contact her husband, tell him
that there was an active shooter at the school, and ask
him to call 911.
A SWAT team eventually arrived and instructed
those who were injured to identify themselves. The
barrage of gunfire killed two students, Nick Dworet
and Helena Ramsay, and injured four others. SWAT
then directed Ms. Schamis and the surviving students
out of the classroom and the building while the
shooter was still inside the school. Outside, Ms.
Schamis saw students running in all directions. Although she lived only about five miles away, she remained near the school and later went to the Marriott,
where students and families had gathered to wait for
news. There, she encountered students bearing the
visible effects of what had happened and witnessed
scenes she described as carnage.
Ms. Schamis returned to teaching after only two
weeks away. She remained at Marjory Stoneman
Douglas High School through the end of the 2017–18
school year so that she could see her seniors graduate,
then stayed another year to see her juniors graduate
in spring 2019. After that graduation, she took a leave
of absence. She was not ready to retire, but she needed
a change. In January 2020, Ms. Schamis and her husband moved to Washington, DC, where she continues
to live. She now works as an office manager at a private school rather than teaching because she felt she
could no longer take responsibility for classroom
safety.

12


The shooting profoundly changed Ms. Schamis’s
sense of safety. She worries about gun violence all the
time and continues to experience ripple effects. She
looks for exits whenever she enters a room and still
has panic attacks in settings that remind her of the
shooting. Under her desk at work, she keeps a very
large bulletproof shield for protection in the event of
an active shooter at the school. She also recalls being
deeply unsettled when, at a mall a few miles from the
school, she encountered a video-game display featuring four life-sized AR-15s. Her service dog, a large
German Shepherd specifically bred and trained to
help her navigate her environment, is an important
part of her life and accompanies her everywhere, including work.
Ms. Schamis remains in contact with former students and with families affected by the shooting,
reaching out on meaningful occasions. She is also a
member of Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence, a
support and advocacy organization that includes educators who survived school shootings in communities
such as Columbine and Sandy Hook. Since the shooting, Ms. Schamis has spoken publicly and given interviews about her experience. She continues to advocate
for policy changes because she believes public policy is
essential to preventing gun violence.
C. Mitch and Annika Dworet
Mitch and Annika Dworet built their family life
around their two sons. They moved to Florida when
their eldest, Nick, was one year old, and raised Nick
and his younger brother, Alex, in an active household
filled with swimming, soccer, karate, and family 5ks.
The family had chosen Parkland specifically because

13


they had heard it was one of the safest places to raise
a family. Mitch had worked in the culinary and hospitality industry for two decades before leaving to transition to a more flexible career in fitness training and
real estate, allowing him to spend more quality time
with his family, which he treasured. Annika was a pediatric nurse. By February 2018, both boys were students at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School.
Nick was 17, a senior, and a gifted swimmer. He had
struggled when he first arrived at a high school of
more than 3,000 students after attending a much
smaller middle school, and he briefly quit swimming
during a difficult freshman year. But he found his
footing. He joined the water polo team, began dating
his girlfriend, took charge of his college applications,
and had just earned a swimming scholarship to the
University of Indianapolis. A captain and district, regional, and state champion, he hoped one day to compete in the Olympics.
Nick and Alex were extremely close. Nick taught
Alex to drive, and the brothers confided in and advised
one another. On February 14, 2018, they were in
classrooms across the hall from each other in the
school’s 1200 building.
That morning, the boys were running late, and
Mitch drove Nick and Alex to school. Near the end of
the day, Nick was in Ms. Schamis’s history class.
Mitch and Annika were running errands at the
neighboring Walmart only minutes from the school
when they realized something was wrong. From the
parking lot, Mitch heard screams and saw students
fleeing the school campus where the Dworets always
thought their two kids would be safe. Then Annika

14


received a call from Alex, who had been grazed in the
head by a bullet and was in an ambulance headed to
North Broward Hospital. She rushed there to find
him. While in the hospital she repeatedly heard hospital staff call “code blue junior” for juvenile patients
in cardiac arrest. Mitch initially remained near the
campus, searching for any information about Nick, before joining Annika amid the chaos at the hospital.
Through the afternoon and evening, they had still
not learned anything certain about Nick. Conflicting
reports circulated, including a rumor that someone
named Nick was at the nearby Marriott where unharmed students were being taken and families of
missing students had gathered. Desperate for answers, Mitch and Annika rushed there and waited for
hours. Parents including the Dworets were instructed
to email their child’s name and photos to assist officers with identification. Each time a cell phone rang,
Annika thought it might bring news of Nick. Neither
parent was willing to believe that, out of thousands of
people on campus, their eldest son had been fatally
shot.
Around two in the morning, the FBI arrived at the
Marriott ballroom. Officers began taking parents
away in pairs, one family at a time, to deliver the
news. Mitch and Annika could hear the cries of other
parents learning that their children had been killed.
About an hour later, the Dworets were taken aside
and told that Nick was among the seventeen people
killed at the school.
In the aftermath, Mitch and Annika had to grieve
Nick while helping Alex recover from physical injuries, nightmares, and post-traumatic stress. They

15


sought therapy for the initial trauma and the grief
that followed, but reminders remain embedded in
daily life: helicopters, clusters of police cars, crowded
places, loud noises, and people carrying large backpacks. Annika stopped attending concerts. On a yoga
retreat years later, even the sound of drums brought
back the fear and helplessness of that day. After 22
years as a pediatric emergency-room nurse, Annika
retired; she no longer wanted to work in a place where
children die.
Annika grew up in Sweden, where gun violence was
rare, and came to the United States without familiarity with American gun culture or the Second Amendment. She and Mitch accept responsible gun ownership, but they also know that assault weapons are
uniquely lethal. After seeing Nick’s autopsy reports
and photographs, Annika understood in the most personal terms the devastating injuries those weapons
can inflict. Mitch has questioned whether Nick might
still be alive if he had been shot with a pistol, but the
assault weapon used left his son with no chance of survival. They are not seeking to repeal the Second
Amendment; they want sensible regulation that recognizes the difference between ordinary firearms and
weapons capable of causing catastrophic harm in seconds.
The helplessness is what the Dworets cannot escape.
Parents teach their children to drive carefully, look
before crossing the street, and make safe choices; they
do not expect that a classroom will be the place where
their child is beyond protection. Mitch and Annika are
still trying to build lives not defined by anger while
honoring Nick, supporting Alex, and urging action

16


that might spare another family the same night of
desperation and lifetime of loss.
D. Anthony Borges
Anthony Borges was 15 years old on February 14,
2018, a freshman at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High
School. Born in Florida and raised in Venezuela, Anthony returned to the United States as a young teenager. Soccer had defined his life since he began playing at age four. He idolized Lionel Messi, played forward, and dreamed of becoming a professional. After
his freshman year, recruiters connected to a Brazilian
training program scouted him, and Anthony accepted
a place. To him, playing professional soccer for Brazil
would have been the fulfillment of a lifelong dream.
That afternoon, Anthony was in a study hall on the
third floor of the school’s 1200 building, with about 10
or 11 other students and a teacher. He sat in a back
corner, waiting for school to let out. He planned on
taking his girlfriend out to the movies for Valentine’s
Day.
Near the end of his last class of the day, shots rang
out through the building. Anthony recognized the
sound from Venezuela, where he had heard guns fired
constantly, but struggled to reconcile it with where he
was. “This can’t be happening,” he thought. Then the
fire alarm sounded. Confused and unaware that the
alarm could be triggered from a shooting, Anthony’s
class moved into the hallway as if for a routine fire
drill.
Anthony headed toward a stairwell at the end of the
hall. The instant he opened the stairwell door, he saw
the rifle. He slammed the door shut, turned, and ran

17


back toward the classroom. A bullet struck his left leg.
He kept moving, reached the crowded room, and
pressed his body against the door as the shooter tried
to get inside and fired through it. Anthony was hit five
times in the legs and back. No one else in the classroom was shot.
When the shooter moved on, Anthony lay on the
floor with his eyes closed, overwhelmed by pain. After
the gunfire stopped, he opened the door. The hallway
was smoky and washed in red light, almost like a horror movie. A girl who had been shot lay nearby. He
tried to speak to her, but she was unresponsive. Anthony felt a gaping wound in his back and saw blood
gushing from his left leg where he’d been shot three
times. He fashioned a tourniquet for his leg as best as
he could and then tried to get on his feet. Unable to
stand, he screamed for help. No one answered.
Anthony lay in the school hallway for nearly an hour
before a SWAT team reached him. By then, he had lost
so much blood that he could barely see. In the ambulance, he just wanted to sleep. At the hospital, everything went black. He remained in a coma for two
weeks.
Anthony spent about two months in the hospital and
underwent 13 surgeries. Doctors removed roughly
one-third of one lung; another bullet had just missed
his liver. Among the injured, Anthony was the most
gravely wounded and the last to leave the hospital.
Even after he was discharged, Anthony struggled
with the physical effects of his injuries. He wasn’t able
to climb the stairs of his modest walk-up apartment,
and so Anthony and his family had to move to a new
home where it would be less difficult to get around.

18


Anthony also needed daily visits from a physical therapist for more than eight months. It took at least a
year before he could walk again, and about a year and
a half before he felt he had regained even half of his
former mobility.
Anthony’s dreams of playing professional soccer
were shattered. Although he pushed himself to return
to the soccer field the following year, he felt like part
of him was gone. Every time he played, it just didn’t
feel the same. Anthony still experiences nerve pain in
his legs almost every day and has learned to organize
ordinary activities around his lasting injuries.
In 2019, Anthony received the Congressional Medal
of Honor Society’s Young Hero Award for his actions
during the shooting.
It took years for Anthony to stop being angry about
the shooting. But even though Anthony has now
turned to a more positive outlook, the shooting stays
with him. Any time he enters a new room, Anthony
looks for potential hiding places and exits. For Anthony, the shooting remains inseparable from his
daily life. “Every day I think about it,” he said. “Everywhere I carry it with me. Everywhere I go.”
E. Stephanie Horowitz
Stephanie Horowitz was 15 years old and a freshman at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School on
February 14, 2018. She loved her outfit that day: a
loose reddish top, jeans, and her favorite jean jacket.
It was Valentine’s Day, and the day started out ordinary: lunch with friends, laughter in acting class, and
videos that still resurface on social media. Before that

19


day, she had only a basic awareness of gun violence
and never imagined it would reach her own life.
By fourth period, Stephanie was in her last class of
the day, finance, in the 700 building, next to the 1200
building. About 20 minutes before the end of class, the
fire alarm went off. The school had held a fire drill
earlier that day, and students had heard talk of a potential active-shooter drill, so Stephanie and her
classmates were confused. Stephanie grabbed her
phone and started toward the parking lot, the designated meeting place for a fire drill.
Outside, she heard the gunshots, but at the time,
she did not know that they were real. She then saw
Coach Aaron Feis on a golf cart telling students to get
back inside.
Back in the classroom, roughly 30 students crowded
into a closet. At first, still unsure what was happening
and thinking that there might be an active shooter
drill, they tried to make light of the situation. Then
they looked on social media and saw reports of an active shooter. The closet went silent, and students began texting friends and telling their parents they
loved them. Stephanie passed around her phone—one
of the few that still had battery life late in the day—
so classmates could call their parents. They remained
in the closet for more than two hours.
When they were finally released, authorities had
blocked the road leading to the school, so parents
could not reach their children and students and teachers stood scattered outside. A neighbor drove Stephanie home. Still unsure whether many of her friends
were safe, she worked through her contacts, texting
everyone she could. She received a few messages

20


about people who had been shot, but did not learn who
had died until after she got home.
Stephanie lost four friends that day: Jaime Guttenberg, Cara Loughran, Luke Hoyer, and Alexander
Schachter. She had known Jaime, Luke, and Alex
since they were little kids. In high school, she shared
a circle of friends with Jaime and Cara. Stephanie also
learned that Coach Feis had been killed.
At home, Stephanie was at a loss for what to do, so
she did what she did at the end of every school day:
she ate an apple. Then she sat on the couch watching
the news and waiting for friends to respond. The next
day, she went to the Parkland Recreation Center,
where students held one another and cried, a pattern
that continued for weeks. Much of that time, and
much of her first three years of high school, remains a
blur.
For years, Stephanie struggled to regain a sense of
safety and normalcy. Survivor’s guilt became so severe that she attempted to take her own life. With
years of intensive therapy, she began to heal, and by
the time she was at Florida State University she no
longer cried, shook, or hid when a balloon popped or
fireworks exploded, although, she still feels pretty
numb. Stephanie thinks she cried enough tears in
high school to last her a lifetime. In 2025, she experienced another school shooting at college.
Today, Stephanie is a second-year law student at
Tulane, channeling her experiences into a determination to help prevent gun violence. She knows firsthand
that the harm does not end when the headline fades:
Friends and family continue to mourn, survivors still
carry fear and guilt, and communities continue

21


grieving long after public attention moves on. Stephanie believes that shootings like these break communities. More than anything, she does not want anyone to
experience what she experienced. She wants to help
bring about the change that might have saved her
friends’ lives, and spared others the lasting trauma
that followed.
F. Robert Schentrup
A few hours’ drive away, Robert Schentrup was in
his freshman dorm at the University of Central Florida in Orlando on February 14, 2018. He and his family, including his two younger sisters, Carmen and
Evelyn, had moved to Parkland about five years prior
because of the Parkland schools’ academic reputation,
and Robert had graduated from Marjory Stoneman
Douglas the year before. That year, while he started
college, both his sisters were at Marjory Stoneman
Douglas, and Carmen would drive her younger sister,
Evelyn, to school almost every day.
When Robert heard that there had been a shooting
at his old high school, he was shocked. He called his
parents frantically, trying to get information about his
sisters, and he worried about his friends and friends’
siblings who were also at the school. Thankfully, he
quickly got ahold of Evelyn who confirmed she wasn’t
hurt, and he took a breath of relief. But no one could
reach Carmen.
For hours, Robert, his family, and Carmen’s friends
desperately tried to find Carmen or anyone with information about her. Robert posted on Facebook begging
for news of her whereabouts. As information slowly
trickled out and he heard about the rising death toll
and saw videos from inside the school, Robert still

22


held onto hope. At first, he hoped that Carmen was
hiding somewhere waiting for the all-clear and that’s
why they hadn’t heard from her. But as the day went
on, that became more and more unlikely.
Finally, after 12 hours of agonizing waiting, Robert’s
dad called him. Through controlled sobs, he said,
“Bobby, your sister has been killed.” Carmen had been
shot while in her AP Psychology class—the same class
Robert had taken just a year before.
Carmen’s death was devastating and unthinkable.
Robert had never thought that gun violence would
touch his life, and certainly never imagined that gun
violence would rip his little sister from his life. Carmen was young, bright, and had a whole life ahead of
her that was stolen from her in an instant. She had a
close-knit group of friends, loved the Marvel universe,
was in the school’s comic book club, and was a gifted
violinist. She was also an extremely talented student.
She was at the top of her class, had been accepted to
attend a prestigious university, and dreamed of pursuing a career in medical research with the hopes of
finding a cure for ALS.
In the wake of the shooting, Robert came to understand just how prevalent mass shootings were in the
United States—and only the United States. Other
countries aren’t plagued by gun violence in the same
way, but the United States’s lax regulations on guns,
and assault weapons in particular, meant that shootings happened more frequently and were more deadly
when they did.
Robert felt compelled to do something and has been
actively involved in preventing gun violence for eight
years. He is a founding member of Team ENOUGH at

23


Brady United, which works to educate young people
about gun violence and mobilize them to take meaningful action to prevent it. And he and his family have
continued to honor Carmen and the life she never got
to live by setting up a fund with the ALS Foundation
to support the work that Carmen will never get to do
herself.
Robert hopes that no one will have to experience the
pain he and his family have suffered losing a loved one
to gun violence.
G. Fred Guttenberg
Fred Guttenberg’s day on February 14, 2018, started
out typically, but it did not end that way. In the afternoon, he received a panicked call from his son, who
was a junior at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High
School. Fred had two children at the school: his son,
and his daughter Jaime, who was 14. His son told him
that there was a shooting and that he had fled the
scene, but he had been unable to reach his sister.
Jaime, Fred says, was tough as nails, and prioritized
being her authentic, passionate, and silly self over
worrying about more-typical teenager concerns. Fred
describes her as the energy in the room wherever she
went. Her passion was dance, and she began competing in it at age nine. She stood up to bullies and joined
multiple organizations that helped children with disabilities form friendships.
Fred told his son to keep running and to let him
worry about Jaime.
Although Fred knew that his daughter was still in
the school, it took him hours to learn that she was shot
and never made it.

24


Jaime had always had a plan, including for the rest
of her life: she knew what she wanted to do (pediatric
physical therapy), and the age by which she wanted to
have children (25). When Jaime was murdered, Fred
and his wife were robbed of their lives with their precious daughter. They will never get to see her embark
on her journey of independence, work on her career,
meet the love of her life, or have children. Fred describes the family’s home as a much quieter place
without Jaime.
Fred has dedicated the rest of his life to ending gun
violence.
CONCLUSION
The judgments of the Second and Seventh Circuits
should be affirmed.
